section.heading: 5.1. Exponential Functions
Exponential Functions and Their Graphs
section.paragraph: Suppose you deposit a sum of $$\$ 1000$$ in an account earning interest at the rate of $$10\%$$ per year compounded continuously (the way most financial institutions compute interest). Then, the accumulated amount at the end of $$t$$ years $$(0 \leq t \leq 20)$$ is described by the function $$f$$ , whose graph appears in Figure 1.* This function is called an exponential function. Observe that the graph of $$f$$ rises rather slowly at first but very rapidly as time goes by. For purposes of comparison, we have also shown the graph of the function $$y = g(t) = 1000\left( {1 + 0.10t} \right)$$ , giving the accumulated amount for the same principal $$(\$ 1000)$$ but earning simple interest at the rate of $$10\%$$ per year. The moral of the story: It is never too early to save.
We will derive the rule for $$f$$ in Section 5.3.

The horizontal axis is labeled t, Years ranges from 0 to around 20 and the vertical axis is labeled y, Dollars ranges from 0 to over 7,000. The first curve y = g(t), starts at the mark 1,000 on the vertical axis, slopes linearly upward to the right, passes through the points (10, 2,000) and (20, 3,000) and extends upwards. The second curve y = f(t) lies above the first curve, starts at the mark 1000 on the vertical axis, veering off the line, goes up to the right and concave upward, passes through around (10, 3,000) and (20, 8,000).

section.paragraph: Exponential functions play an important role in mathematical analysis. Because of their special characteristics, they are some of the most useful functions and are found in virtually every field in which mathematics is applied. To mention a few examples: Under ideal conditions, the number of bacteria present at any time $$t$$ in a culture may be described by an exponential function of $$t$$ ; radioactive substances decay over time in accordance with an “exponential” law of decay; money left on fixed deposit and earning compound interest grows exponentially; and some of the most important distribution functions encountered in statistics are exponential.
Let’s begin our investigation into the properties of exponential functions by studying their graphs.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the exponential function $$y = 2^{x}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, as was discussed earlier, the domain of the exponential function $$y = f(x) = 2^{x}$$ is the set of real numbers. Next, putting $$x = 0$$ gives $$y = 2^{0} = 1$$ , the $$y$$ -intercept of $$f$$ . There is no $$x$$ -intercept, since there is no value of $$x$$ for which $$y = 0$$ . To find the range of $$f$$ , consider the following table of values:

We see from these computations that $$2^{x}$$ decreases and approaches zero as $$x$$ decreases without bound and that $$2^{x}$$ increases without bound as $$x$$ increases without bound. Thus, the range of $$f$$ is the interval $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ —that is, the set of positive real numbers. Finally, we sketch the graph of $$y = f(x) = 2^{x}$$ in Figure 2.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the exponential function $$y = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The domain of the exponential function $$y = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ is the set of all real numbers. The $$y$$ -intercept is $$\left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{0} = 1$$ ; there is no $$x$$ -intercept, since there is no value of $$x$$ for which $$y = 0$$ . From the following table of values

we deduce that $$\left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x} = {1 \slash 2}^{x}$$ increases without bound as $$x$$ decreases without bound and that $$\left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ decreases and approaches zero as $$x$$ increases without bound. Thus, the range of $$f$$ is the interval $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . The graph of $$y = f(x) = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ is sketched in Figure 3.

section.paragraph: The functions $$y = 2^{x}$$ and $$y = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ , whose graphs you studied in Examples 3 and 4, are special cases of the exponential function $$y = f(x) = b^{x}$$ , obtained by setting $$b = 2$$ and $$b = {1 \slash 2}$$ , respectively. In general, the exponential function $$y = b^{x}$$ with $$b > 1$$ has a graph similar to that of $$y = 2^{x}$$ , whereas the graph of $$y = b^{x}$$ for $$0 < b < 1$$ is similar to that of $$y = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ (Exercises 27 and 28). When $$b = 1$$ , the function $$y = b^{x}$$ reduces to the constant function $$y = 1$$ . For comparison, the graphs of all three functions are sketched in Figure 4.

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The first curve y = b^x (b > 1) enters the second quadrant running almost parallel to the x axis, rising slightly upward to the right, concave up, cuts the y axis enters the first quadrant, rises up to the right, concave up, and extends further. The second curve y = b^x (0 < b < 1) enters the second quadrant at the top, slopes downward to the right, concave up, cuts the y axis, enters the first quadrant, slopes down to the right, and concave up, running almost parallel to the x axis and extends further. Both the curves intersect the horizontal line y = 1.

figure.caption: $$y = b^{x}$$ is an increasing function of $$x$$ if $$b > 1$$ , a constant function if $$b = 1$$ , and a decreasing function if $$0 < b < 1$$ .

note.title: Properties of the Exponential Function
note.heading: Properties of the Exponential Function
note.paragraph: The exponential function $$y = b^{x}\left( {b > 0,b \neq 1} \right)$$ has the following properties:

list.item: Its graph passes through the point $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ .
It is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b > 1$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ if $$b < 1$$ .

section.paragraph: Next, we consider another exponential function to the base $$e$$ that is closely related to the previous function and is particularly useful in constructing models that describe “exponential decay.”

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the function $$y = e^{- x}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Since $$e > 1$$ , it follows that $$0 < {1 \slash e} < 1$$ , so $$f(x) = e^{- x} = {1 \slash e^{x}} = \left( {1 \slash e} \right)^{x}$$ is an exponential function with base less than $$1$$ . Therefore, it has a graph similar to that of the exponential function $$y = \left( {1 \slash 2} \right)^{x}$$ . section.heading: Using Technology
section.paragraph: Although the proof is outside the scope of this book, it can be proved that an exponential function of the form $$f(x) = b^{x}$$ , where $$b > 1$$ , will ultimately grow faster than the power function $$g(x) = x^{n}$$ for any positive real number $$n$$ . To give a visual demonstration of this result for the special case of the exponential function $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ , we can use a graphing utility to plot the graphs of both $$f$$ and $$g$$ (for selected values of $$n$$ ) on the same set of axes in an appropriate viewing window and observe that the graph of $$f$$ ultimately lies above that of $$g$$ .
